Finger-length whole fish, eaten bones and all with a squeeze of lemon.
Wheat wrapper, deep fried.

items.en: Chicken tenderloin wrapped with shiso leaf

A Kyoto speciality — the silky film lifted off simmering soy milk, eaten cold with a dab of soy and wasabi. The soy skin itself is fine; the dipping sauce is the wheat risk, and it may be dashi-based rather than plain soy.
Whole garlic cloves cured in a red-shiso pickle — sharp, sweet-sour, a drinking snack. Pickling liquid often contains soy sauce or bonito extract.
Yes, whale — still an old-school izakaya staple in Japan. Dark, dense, beef-like meat simmered in soy and ginger. Worth knowing what you are ordering.

items.en: Pacific saury simmered with sansho pepper

items.en: Fermented soybeans with grated mountain yam

Cold pink duck breast fanned over leaves. The dressing is the gluten question.

Charred whole until collapsing, skin slipped off, served with ginger and soy. Almost always finished with bonito flakes.
A sac of tiny salted roe, spicy and intensely savoury — eaten in small bites with rice or drink. The curing liquid usually contains soy and sometimes wheat.
A Kansai variety so tender and juicy it is eaten raw, torn by hand. Usually served with a soy or dashi dip.
A block of firm tofu fried so the outside is golden and chewy, then grilled and topped with ginger and spring onion. Plant-based in itself — the poured-over sauce and bonito flakes are what break it.

items.note: The whole shop is this bowl. Broth built on dried baby sardines with heads and guts left in, so it keeps a real bitter edge — oceanic and savoury, the taste niboshi fans chase and everyone else finds strange. A whole dried sardine sits on top as a garnish. The shop romanises its name NIBO-TAMA on the menu.

items.en: Deluxe niboshi ramen — same bowl plus 3 sheets of nori and a marinated egg
items.note: 特製 (tokusei, 'special') on almost any Japanese ramen menu means the loaded version. Here the extra ¥300 buys exactly 3 sheets of nori and one ajitama.

items.en: Brothless niboshi noodles — noodles tossed in seasoned oil and tare
items.note: 油そば (abura-soba) arrives with no soup: a pool of flavoured oil and tare at the bottom of the bowl. Mix hard from the bottom before the first bite. The table vinegar and chilli are meant for it.
大盛り (oomori) = extra noodles. Here it costs nothing, so say 大盛りで (oomori de) when you order if you are hungry. 並 (nami) would be the regular size.
Also written 味玉 (ajitama) at most shops — a jammy-yolked egg steeped in soy tare. The single most-ordered ramen topping in Japan.
Dip a sheet into the broth to soften, then wrap a mouthful of noodles in it.
A heap of raw sliced green onion — cuts through the oil of a niboshi bowl.
Ferociously sour and salty. Unusual on ramen — it works with the sardine broth. Some are cured with bonito or soy.
Japanese-market kimchi commonly contains fish sauce or salted shrimp, and the seasoning can carry wheat.
The braised pork belly or loin slices. On most menus the pre-loaded version is called チャーシュー麺.
Melts into the oil of the abura-soba rather than the ramen — that is how regulars use it.

items.en: Rare-cooked pork over rice, small bowl
items.note: 生 here means the pork is cooked low and slow so it stays pink and soft, laid over rice with a yolk. A ¥500 mini bowl, not a full meal.

items.en: Rice topped with dried sardine, nori and chilli
items.note: いりこ is the western-Japan word for the same dried sardines the broth is made from. The house move: eat half, then tip the rest into the leftover ramen broth.
卵かけご飯 abbreviated. Crack the raw egg on hot rice, add the soy tare, stir until glossy. A national comfort food — eggs are safe to eat raw in Japan. The tare is wheat soy.
Barley-based, so not gluten-free.

items.note: ¥1,400 for 300g. A rotating limited — on the wall when it is on.

items.en: The everything topping — extra pork, extra spring onion and a marinated egg
items.note: Common to こってり and あっさり. This is the shop's 全部のせ (zenbu-nose, 'put it all on'). On 濃厚とりとん the equivalent is called 特製 and also costs ¥600.
マシ (mashi) = more. The pork is a shoulder-cut chashu; for a stretch of 2026 it was made from named Shonan Miyaji-buta pork.
Raw sliced green onion, to cut the fat of a very heavy bowl.
Already included in the price of 濃厚とりとん.

items.ja: 無料トッピング（高菜・紅生姜・無限ニンニク）
items.en: Free toppings: pickled mustard greens, red pickled ginger, bottomless garlic
items.note: Help yourself at the counter. 無限ニンニク literally means 'infinite garlic'. A fourth free item, 赤ガッパ (a chashu-offcut relish), was suspended indefinitely in July 2026. Takana and beni-shoga are usually seasoned with soy and sometimes contain fish extract.

items.en: A bowl of plain rice, self-service
items.note: One bowlful, taken yourself from the rice cooker — not free refills. Plain unseasoned rice, so genuinely gluten-free and vegan on its own. The shop is fussy about its rice and names the producer on its blog.
The standard bottled tea; unsweetened and slightly bitter.
Not served to anyone driving a car or motorbike.

kyr_menya_sawaki.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off the shop's own laminated menu card (photo dated ~2026-04) and the student-set card (~2026-07); a 2026-05 diner confirmed ¥850 for the small iekei. Cash only, all prices tax-included.

items.section: 家系ラーメン / Iekei ramen
items.note: The house speciality and the only proper iekei shop in Ichijoji. Iekei idiom: pork-bone broth cut with a soy tare, thick straight noodles, spinach, a couple of shoulder-loin chashu, wood-ear, white onion, and — unusually for Kyoto — a quail egg, plus two sheets of nori you dunk in the broth and wrap around rice. You'll be asked three things: 麺の硬さ (noodle firmness — かため katame / 普通 futsū / やわめ yawame), 味の濃さ (tare strength — 濃いめ koime / 普通 / 薄め usume) and 油の量 (back-fat — 多め ōme / 普通 / 少なめ sukuname). Saying 「普通で」 (futsū de, 'normal') for all three is completely fine. 'Small' here is 150 g, i.e. a normal bowl elsewhere.

items.section: 家系ラーメン / Iekei ramen
items.note: Same bowl, 200 g of noodles. 小/中/大 (shō/chū/dai) is the small/medium/large ladder — here it only changes the noodle weight, not the toppings.

items.section: 家系ラーメン / Iekei ramen
items.note: 300 g — a serious portion. Noodles are a custom order from Gotō Seimen (est. 1948) and, unusually for iekei, are left full-length rather than cut short.

items.en: Extra pork (chashu upgrade on any bowl)
items.section: 家系ラーメン / Iekei ramen
items.note: 'Niku-mashi' = more meat. It's priced as a whole bowl, not a supplement: ¥1,100 with the 150 g, ¥1,150 with 200 g, ¥1,200 with 300 g, and ¥1,100 on any of the non-iekei bowls. The chashu is shoulder loin steeped in the soy tare — sweet and well soaked.

items.ja: チャルメララーメン（普通麺or細麺）
items.en: Light, clear 'tanrei' style ramen — the old street-vendor taste
items.note: 淡麗 (tanrei) means clear and delicate, the opposite of the iekei bowl. 'Charumera' is the little reed horn Japan's night-time ramen carts used to honk — the name is pure nostalgia. Pick 普通麺 (futsū-men, regular) or 細麺 (hoso-men, thin). Limited quantity daily (数量限定).

屋台 = a food stall; this is the Fukuoka idiom — milky tonkotsu with hair-thin noodles. You choose firmness from the Hakata ladder, hardest first: コナ (kona, barely cooked) ・ハリガネ (harigane, 'wire') ・バリカタ (barikata, very firm) ・カタ (kata, firm) ・ノーマル (normal) ・ヤワ (yawa, soft). Barikata is the local default.

Same tonkotsu broth as the yatai bowl but with normal-thickness noodles, so no firmness call needed. This shop was a Hakata tonkotsu specialist before it converted to iekei in Oct 2023 — these bowls are the survivors of that menu.
昔ながらの (mukashi-nagara no) = 'the way it always was' — a plain brown soy broth, the Shōwa-era shokudō taste. Limited quantity.

Shio = salt rather than soy as the seasoning, so the broth stays pale. Salt tare still usually contains some soy or dashi, so it's an 'ask' at best — and the wheat noodles put the bowl out of reach regardless.

items.en: Kyoto 'black' ramen — very dark soy broth
items.section: 京都醤油系 / Kyoto soy style
items.note: Kyoto's own dark-soy lineage (the Shinpuku-saikan idiom): a broth so soy-dark it looks like ink, saltier and sharper than it looks, heaped with green onion. Sells out (売切れごめん — 'sorry when it's gone').
大盛 (ōmori) is the standard word for 'large portion' on any Japanese menu.

items.en: Second helping of noodles, added to your remaining broth
items.note: The Hakata custom: eat the noodles fast, then call 「替玉お願いします」 (kaedama onegaishimasu) while there's still soup left and a fresh nest arrives. Leave enough broth.

items.ja: お好きなラーメン＋唐揚3コ＋ごはん（小・並）
items.en: Set: any ramen + 3 pieces of fried chicken + rice
items.section: お得なセットメニュー / Set add-ons
items.note: ¥380 is the ADD-ON price on top of whichever bowl you ordered, not the total. Rice comes small (小) or regular (並); large rice is +¥50.

items.ja: お好きなラーメン＋もつ煮＋ごはん（小・並）
items.en: Set: any ramen + simmered pork offal + rice
items.section: お得なセットメニュー / Set add-ons
items.note: もつ煮 (motsu-ni) is pork or beef offal stewed soft in miso or soy — a cheap, deeply savoury izakaya staple. Add-on price.

items.ja: お好きなラーメン＋人気の自家製そぼろ丼
items.en: Set: any ramen + house minced-pork rice bowl
items.section: お得なセットメニュー / Set add-ons
items.note: そぼろ (soboro) is meat minced and dry-simmered in sweet soy until crumbly, spooned over rice. Add-on price.

items.ja: 本日のラーメン　ランチセット
items.en: Lunch set — today's ramen plus a side
items.section: お得なセットメニュー / Set add-ons
items.note: 本日の = 'today's'. A fixed-price lunch deal built round whatever bowl the shop is pushing that day.

items.ja: 学割メニュー（学生さん応援）
items.en: Student deal: any ramen + a rice or noodle add-on
items.section: お得なセットメニュー / Set add-ons
items.note: 学割 = student discount, high-school age and up, student ID shown BEFORE ordering. Step 1: pick a ramen (iekei small or medium, charumera, shoyu, shio, yatai, Hakata chuka-soba, Kyoto black, or the summer-only zaru ramen). Step 2: pick one of — ① karaage or motsu-ni with rice, ② extra noodles or a kaedama plus rice (not available with iekei), ③ a flavoured rice (bonito-flake, salmon, or kimchi). Ichijoji is a student district; this is why.
Marinated in soy and ginger, dusted in starch and flour, deep-fried. The half portion 唐揚ハーフ（3ケ）is ¥380 — '3ケ' just means three pieces.
水ギョーザ = boiled rather than pan-fried gyoza — softer, slippery wrappers. 一口 (hitokuchi) = one-bite size.
Ordered on its own rather than as part of a set.

items.ja: 自家製こまぎれチャーシュー旨煮丼
items.en: Rice bowl of chopped house chashu simmered in its tare
items.note: こまぎれ = the offcuts, chopped small; 旨煮 = simmered in a sweet-savoury soy braise. Sells out.

items.ja: 濃厚玉子かけごはん　並
items.note: TKG — a raw egg cracked over hot rice with a splash of soy, stirred to a custard. Large (大) ¥300. The soy is the gluten question.

Unseasoned steamed rice — genuinely gluten-free and vegan as long as nothing is poured on it. Medium ¥200, large ¥250. In an iekei shop the standard move is to dunk a sheet of nori in the broth, lay it on the rice with a dab of the counter-top grated garlic, and wrap.
Free on request. Other toppings are ¥100 each — のり nori, メンマ menma (fermented bamboo), うずら quail egg, キムチ kimchi, 青ねぎ green onion, きくらげ wood-ear mushroom — and ホウレン草 spinach ¥200.

kyr_ramen_yume.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read directly off the shop's ticket machine in a photo from a March 2026 visit, and cross-checked against diners who paid ¥1,000 for the puchi (Nov 2025) and ¥1,200 for the dai (Jan 2026). Cash only.

items.ja: プチ ラーメン（麺量200g）
items.note: Buy a ticket at the machine by the entrance BEFORE you sit — at busy times buy it first and wait in the corridor. Jiro-style ('Jiro-kei') means a thick, non-emulsified pork broth with a sweet-sharp soy edge, very fat chewy noodles, a mountain of boiled beansprouts and cabbage, chunks of soft stewed pork and a slick of back-fat. 200 g is the smallest normal size and still a lot of food; the owner also added an even smaller プチプチ (150 g) at some point.
Careful: 小 ('small') in a Jiro-style shop is 300 g — the size a normal ramen shop would call regular. Two slices of pork come as standard.
400 g of noodles. Only order this if you've done Jiro before.
500 g. The half-kilo tier.

items.ja: プチ 豚ラーメン（麺量200g）
items.en: Pork ramen, 200 g — five slices of stewed pork instead of two
items.note: 豚 (buta) on a Jiro-style machine means the extra-pork version: 5 slices rather than the standard 2. Yume's pork is stewed soft and cut chunky — rock-like slabs that fall apart. Same size ladder: 小 300 g ¥1,400, 並 400 g ¥1,450, 大 500 g ¥1,500.

items.ja: 小 豚ラーメン（麺量300g）
items.note: The most-ordered bowl here — 300 g plus the five pork slices.

items.ja: 並 豚ラーメン（麺量400g）
大 豚ラーメン（麺量500g）

items.note: 限定 (gentei) = a rotating one-off the owner is running that day; there's no way to know what it is except by asking or looking at the shop's X account (@yume_sora04). Same four sizes: 小 300 g ¥1,300, 並 400 g ¥1,350, 大 500 g ¥1,400.

items.en: Soupless — the same bowl built as a stir-together noodle dish
items.note: 汁なし literally 'no soup': noodles, vegetables, pork and fat with concentrated tare at the bottom, which you turn over and mix. Sold in the same four sizes (200/300/400/500 g) and, per the machine layout, at the same prices as the soup bowls — the tiles were not sharp enough in the photo to read with certainty, so check the machine. A 豚汁なし (extra-pork soupless) row exists too.

items.ja: ニンニク・ヤサイ・アブラ・カラメ（無料コール）
items.en: The free counter call — garlic, veg, fat, seasoning strength
items.note: THE thing to know before you sit down. As your bowl is plated the staff will ask about four things and the sign says the price never changes. 「ニンニク入れますか？」 'Garlic in?' — answer あり (ari, yes) / なし (nashi, no) / 少なめ (sukuname, a little) / マシ (mashi, more) / マシマシ (mashi-mashi, loads). Same scale for 野菜 (yasai, the beansprout-and-cabbage pile) and アブラ (abura, pork back-fat). カラメ (karame) means crank up the soy seasoning. If you don't want to think about it, the sign explicitly says just answering ari or nashi on garlic is enough — or say 「普通で」. Staff do double-check first-timers who ask for yasai-mashi, and they're right to. Note: the vegetables are cooked in the pork pot, so nothing here is vegetarian.
Bought as a ticket at the machine, not called at the counter.

items.en: Extra pork ticket — three more slices
items.note: Each buta-mashi ticket adds three more slices on top of whatever you ordered. The price tile was not legible in the photo (it was ¥250 in 2024); check the machine.
A common Jiro-style trick — it melts into the fat and rounds off the salt.

items.ja: トッピングA / トッピングB
items.en: Paid topping tier A (¥50) and tier B (¥100)
items.note: Two generic buttons; what's in each tier is written on cards beside the machine and changes. Fried onion (フライドオニオン) and fish powder (魚粉, gyofun — dried-fish powder, so not vegan) have both been options.

items.en: A scoop of rice to finish in the leftover broth
items.note: Plain rice tipped into what's left of the bowl at the end. The rice itself is gluten-free and vegan; the broth it lands in is neither. Price not legible on the machine photo.

kyr_shirakawa.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Taken from the shop's own handwritten お品書き card photographed on an October 2025 visit; a January 2025 diner independently paid ¥700 for the ramen and ¥950 for the ramen-and-fried-rice set.

items.note: This is Kyoto's own chuka-soba idiom, the 背脂チャッチャ (se-abura chattcha) style: a clear pork-and-chicken soy broth with pearls of pork back-fat flicked over the surface, thin straight noodles, thin-sliced pork belly chashu, menma and a heap of green onion. Shirakawa's twist is a noticeable dose of vinegar already in the broth, which rounds it out. The famous ancestor of the style, ますたに, is three minutes' walk away. You can ask for かため (katame, firm noodles). Ichimi chilli, black pepper and a vinegar cruet sit on the table — locals add more vinegar.

items.en: Kyoto-style soy ramen, large (1.5 portions of noodles)
items.note: 玉 (tama) is the counter for a nest of noodles, so 1.5玉 is one-and-a-half servings.

items.en: Kyoto-style soy ramen, extra-large (2 portions of noodles)
items.note: 特大 (tokudai) = 'extra large', double noodles.

items.ja: チャーシューメン　並
items.en: Same ramen buried under extra pork slices, regular
items.note: チャーシューメン on any Japanese ramen menu means the identical bowl with the chashu count multiplied. Here it's thin-sliced pork belly.

items.ja: チャーシューメン　大（1.5玉）
items.en: Extra-pork ramen, large (1.5 portions of noodles)
items.note: The 特大 (2玉) tier exists too but its price was hidden behind a napkin stand in the photograph — expect roughly ¥1,200.

items.ja: ラーメン＋小チャーハンセット
items.en: Ramen with a small fried rice
items.note: Not printed on the laminated card but consistently reported by diners in Nov 2023, Jan 2025 and Dec 2025. チャーハン (chāhan) — also written ヤキメシ/焼めし in Kansai — is soy-seasoned Chinese fried rice, here light and grainy and about a half portion. Under ¥1,000 for both, which is why locals order it. Soy sauce means fried rice is never gluten-free.
Unseasoned steamed rice — genuinely gluten-free and vegan on its own. Regular ¥200, large (大, described on the card as 2杯分, 'two bowls' worth') ¥300.

items.en: Plain white rice, large (two bowls' worth)

items.note: 生 (nama) = draft. 中 is the standard mug.

kyr_raamen_sakurai.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Transcribed from the shop's own printed menu card photographed around late 2025, and matched to diners who paid ¥950 (Oct/Nov 2025) and ¥1,150 (Apr 2026). An English-language menu is available — ask. Open until 2 a.m., so it works as a post-drinks bowl.

items.ja: 鶏出汁しょうゆらぁ麺
items.note: The shop's headline bowl and the one to order first. Domestic chicken simmered gently to a clear golden 清湯 (chintan) broth, seasoned with a blend of four soy sauces including twice-brewed 再仕込 and twice-aged shoyu. Thin firm noodles (細麺). Toppings are white Kanto-style long onion, chicken-breast chashu and Kyoto-pork shoulder loin. The card states no MSG, preservatives or additives anywhere in the broth. Several diners describe the tare as sweet, closer to a Japanese soba broth than a typical ramen.

items.ja: 鶏白湯しょうゆらぁ麺
items.note: 白湯 (paitan) means the bones were boiled hard until the broth went opaque and creamy — the chicken equivalent of tonkotsu, here 7+ hours, blended with soy from three old Kyoto soy brewers. Served with chewy medium-thick noodles (中太麺). The kitchen aerates it with a spuma whipper so it arrives foamy.

Same creamy chicken base, seasoned with a barley-miso-led blend of three misos. Worth knowing: 麦味噌 (mugi-miso) is barley miso, so this bowl carries gluten from the miso as well as the noodles. Medium-thick noodles.

The richest bowl on the card: roasted sesame paste blended with three additive-free chilli-sesame seasonings, cut into the thick chicken paitan. Medium-thick noodles. Described on the card as 'kotteri' — heavy.

items.en: Half a fresh nest of noodles for your leftover broth
items.note: Call 「替え玉お願いします」 (kaedama onegaishimasu) while you still have soup. Unusually, this shop lets you choose which noodle comes back: 細麺 (thin), 中太麺 (medium-thick) or 極太平麺 (very thick flat) — so you can change texture mid-meal.

items.en: A full fresh nest of noodles
items.note: Same three noodle choices as the half portion.
Usually shortened to 味玉 (ajitama) — a jammy-yolked egg steeped in soy and mirin. The marinade is the gluten question.

items.ja: 鶏ムネチャーシュー（3枚）
items.note: ムネ = breast. Cooked low and slow, so it stays pale pink and moist rather than roasted.

items.ja: 京都ポーク肩ロース（3枚）
items.en: Three slices of Kyoto-brand pork shoulder loin
items.note: 肩ロース = shoulder loin, the cut with just enough fat to stay tender.

items.en: Double chashu — two chicken plus two pork slices
items.note: W is read 'daburu' (double); 各2枚 = two of each.

items.en: A pile of shredded white long onion
items.note: The shop deliberately uses the Kanto-style white long onion, which is rare in Kansai, because it stands up to the dark soy.
Plain toasted nori is naturally gluten-free, but it goes straight into a wheat-noodle bowl, so it's academic here.
激辛 = seriously hot. 秘伝 = a secret recipe.
Unseasoned steamed rice — genuinely gluten-free and vegan.

items.en: Rice with spicy marinated pollock roe
items.note: 明太子 (mentaiko) is pollock roe cured with chilli — salty, faintly fishy, granular. The cure usually contains soy and sometimes wheat.
TKG — crack the egg on the hot rice, add the soy provided, stir until it goes silky. A completely normal thing to eat in Japan.
Also sold as an 炙り (aburi, blowtorch-seared) version.

items.en: 'Dive rice' — rice to tip into your leftover broth
items.note: The finish move: 'dive' the rice into what's left of the soup and eat it as a porridge. Rice itself is fine; the broth it lands in is not.
Japanese commercial kimchi very often contains fish sauce or dried shrimp, and the seasoning can contain wheat.

items.ja: チャーシュー盛り合わせ
items.note: 盛り合わせ = an assortment. A drinking snack — this place runs till 2 a.m.

items.en: 'Mouth-watering chicken' — cold poached chicken in chilli-sesame sauce
items.note: A Sichuan classic (kou shui ji). The sauce is soy, chilli oil, sesame and vinegar — soy means gluten unless confirmed otherwise.
炙り (aburi) means the surface is scorched with a torch just before serving.
水 = boiled rather than pan-fried, so the wrappers stay soft and slippery. 個 (ko) is the counter for pieces.
Bottled beer (瓶ビール) is ¥600; the various shochu highballs — chuhai, whisky highball, oolong-, green-tea-, hojicha- and jasmine-shochu — are ¥550 each. Cola ¥300, orange juice ¥250.

kyr_chuka_soba_onigiri_maru_.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off the shop's own street sign (May 2025) and its touchscreen ticket machine (May 2025 and May 2026 photos); a May 2026 diner confirms ¥900 for the ginger chuka-soba and ¥150 for a large portion. Cash only.

items.ja: 熟成醤油の生姜中華そば
items.en: Aged-soy chicken ramen scented with ginger — the house No.1
items.note: 中華そば literally 'Chinese noodles' — the older, homelier word for ramen. The broth is domestic chicken plus stewing hens and seven vegetables, kept clear, with a tare of three blended aged soy sauces and a ginger-infused aroma oil floated on top. Toppings: two big thin slices of low-temperature-cooked shoulder-loin rare chashu, menma, green onion and chopped red onion. Noodles are made for the shop alone from Aichi wheat ('Ayuchi no Minori') with natural kansui — thin, low-hydration and springy. Large portion (大盛り) +¥150.

items.ja: 淡泊醤油の貝ダシ中華そば
items.en: Pale-soy ramen in a clam-and-scallop broth
items.note: 貝ダシ = shellfish stock — asari clams and scallop over a base of domestic chicken, flying-fish niboshi and Rishiri kelp, seasoned with a blend of Inner Mongolian and Okinawan salt. Comes with rare chashu, two fat menma, chopped onion and green onion, and — importantly — a thin slice of lemon, whose acidity is what makes the bowl work. Gentle rather than briny.

items.en: Soy ramen with pork back-fat, plus chunks of braised pork belly
items.note: 背脂 (se-abura) is pork back-fat, minced and scattered over the surface — the signature of Kyoto's own chuka-soba idiom. Started as a limited special and became permanent. Alongside the thin rare chashu you get about three fat cubes of soft braised pork belly, menma and green onion. The fat is applied with restraint here, not the full 'chattcha' blizzard.

items.ja: 熟成醤油の籠つけそば
items.en: Dipping noodles served on a bamboo tray
items.note: つけそば/つけ麺 = the noodles come cold on the side (here in a 籠, a little wooden basket-tray) and you dip them a few at a time into a small bowl of hot concentrated broth. Aged-soy tare with dried-sardine (niboshi) aroma. Sets: +onigiri ¥1,180, +karaage ¥1,180, both ¥1,410.

items.ja: 秘伝の割りドの籠肉つけそば
items.note: The meat-loaded version of the tray tsukemen. 割りド refers to the 割りスープ — the thin soup they'll top your dipping broth up with at the end so you can drink it. Priced above the plain tsuke-soba; check the machine (it was ¥1,100 at opening).

items.ja: TKM タマゴかけ麺（追い飯無料）
items.en: 'Egg-over-noodles' — soupless noodles with a raw yolk, free rice to finish
items.note: A pun on 卵かけご飯 (raw egg over rice), swapping in noodles. Soupless noodles with a raw egg, bonito flakes, green onion and rare chashu — stir it all together. 追い飯無料 means the finishing scoop of rice is free: tip it into whatever's left and eat it as a second course. Sets: +onigiri ¥1,130, +karaage ¥1,130, both ¥1,360.

items.ja: TKM【おにぎり&からあげセット】
items.en: Egg-noodles with both a rice ball and fried chicken
items.note: The pattern across the whole machine: any bowl +¥230 for an onigiri, +¥230 for the karaage, +¥460 for both.

items.ja: いりこ出汁薫る 淡涼冷やしそば
items.en: Summer-only chilled noodles in dried-sardine broth
items.note: 夏季限定 = summer only, and it was running in August 2026. Iriko (dried sardine) from Ibukijima in Kagawa, made into a clear cold dashi, with rare chashu, a marinated egg, tomato, sudachi citrus and sprouts over ice-tightened noodles.

items.en: Onigiri: fresh bonito flakes with soy
items.note: The whole point of the shop's onigiri is that they are NOT squeezed tight — they're loosely formed to order, so they're huge and cloud-light (and slightly hard to bite through). Rice is specially-grown Akitakomachi shipped from Ogata-mura in Niigata. Okaka = bonito flakes dressed with soy sauce. The house recommendation is to save half your onigiri and drop it into the leftover ramen broth as a zosui/ochazuke finish.
昆布 here means kombu no tsukudani — kelp simmered down in soy and mirin until dark and sticky. Soy is the gluten question; check the truffle element isn't butter-based.

items.en: Onigiri: salmon with salmon roe ('parent and child')
items.note: 親子 (oyako, 'parent and child') is the standard Japanese joke for pairing a fish or bird with its own eggs. すじこ is roe still in the membrane, saltier and denser than loose ikura.

items.ja: レアチャーシュー卵黄
items.en: Onigiri: rare chashu with a cured egg yolk
items.note: The chashu offcuts are folded inside and a marinated yolk sits on top. The most-recommended of the four.

items.en: Fried chicken tossed in bonito furikake
items.note: まぶし = 'dusted/rolled in'. Ginger-marinated chicken tatsuta-age, then rolled in a dried-bonito seasoning — savoury enough to eat with plain rice rather than as a ramen side. Three pieces in the set version. It was ¥480 at opening; the current à-la-carte price wasn't legible.
The topping tab on the machine also carries 生たまご (raw egg), チャーシュー, メンマ (fermented bamboo shoot), ネギ (green onion) and 玉ねぎ (onion).
Diners warn these low-hydration noodles soften fast, so a large portion can go slack before you finish it.

items.ja: 昆布酢 / ハラペーニョ酢 / 一味唐辛子 / 和山椒
items.en: Table condiments: kelp vinegar, jalapeño vinegar, chilli powder, Japanese sanshō pepper
items.note: They're matched to specific dishes, and the tray card tells you which. Kelp vinegar (apple vinegar steeped with kombu, sweet-sour) and ichimi chilli go with the ginger chuka-soba; the hot jalapeño vinegar is meant for the TKM; sanshō — the tingly, citrus-numbing Japanese peppercorn — is for the tsuke-soba. Kelp vinegar is the one most people rate. Go easy: over-dosing them flattens the broth.

items.ja: 瓶ビール / ハイボール / レモンサワー
items.en: Bottled beer, whisky highball, lemon sour
items.note: Listed on the street sign's drink panel; prices weren't legible in the photograph.

kyr_sarashina_shogoin_shiten.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Transcribed from the shop's own yellow MENU card photographed on a visit in early 2026; the card carries this branch's phone number (751-1931), matching the Shogoin-Higashimachi address, so it is the right Sarashina — the name is common nationwide. Cash. Note the shop is at the end of a covered alley barely a metre wide; the standing sign outside reads 「奥で営業しております」 ('we're open, down the back').

items.en: Old-school Kyoto Chinese noodles in a light broth
items.note: The reason to come. 中華そば is the pre-war word for ramen and in a Kyoto 麺類店 like this it means something gentler than a ramen shop's version: a pale, faintly dashi-ish soy broth, white straight noodles, and a topping set that gives the game away — chashu, menma, green onion, nori, a slice of grilled kamaboko fishcake and 梅麩 (ume-fu), plum-blossom-shaped wheat gluten, which is a Kyoto noodle-shop garnish, not a ramen one. Ground pepper is dusted over before it leaves the kitchen and it arrives with a wooden renge. Note the 麸 is pure wheat gluten on top of the wheat noodles.

items.en: The same bowl, upgraded with more pork
items.note: （上）(jō) is the standard Japanese grade marker meaning 'superior' — on this menu it buys you extra chashu, five or six thin slices of gently braised pork rather than the usual couple.

The base bowl — soft thick wheat noodles in a pale kelp-and-bonito broth, which in Kyoto is lighter-coloured and less soy-forward than Tokyo's. The bonito dashi makes it non-vegan, and udon is wheat by definition.

items.en: Plain buckwheat noodles in the same broth
items.note: Every dish on the 麺類 list can be had as either udon or soba at the same price — just say 「そばで」 (soba de) or 「うどんで」. Restaurant soba is almost always cut with wheat flour, so it is not a gluten-free option.

items.en: Noodles topped with sweet simmered fried tofu
items.note: きつね ('fox') = 油揚げ (abura-age), a sheet of thin deep-fried tofu simmered in sweet soy until it's a sponge full of sweet broth. Named for the fox-god's supposed fondness for it. Tofu is soy, the broth is bonito — so not vegan, and the soy is not gluten-free.

items.en: KYOTO tanuki — fried tofu and onion in a thick gingered broth
items.note: A genuine trap for travellers. In Tokyo たぬき means crunchy tempura batter bits; in Osaka it means kitsune-on-soba. In KYOTO it means the kitsune toppings served in an あんかけ — a broth thickened with kuzu or potato starch into a glossy sauce — with grated ginger on top. Completely different dish, same three letters. It stays scaldingly hot; eat carefully.

items.en: Noodles in a thickened, glossy starch broth
items.note: あんかけ is the technique itself — dashi thickened with starch so it clings to the noodles and holds heat. A Kyoto winter staple, usually finished with ginger.

items.en: Noodles with egg swirled through the broth and set
items.note: とじ (toji) means 'to bind/close' — beaten egg poured over the simmering broth so it sets in soft ribbons across the surface. You'll see the word again on several dishes below; it always means this.

items.en: 'Moon-viewing' — a raw egg cracked whole on top
items.note: The intact yellow yolk sitting on the noodles is the moon. It poaches slowly in the hot broth; break it when you feel like it.

items.en: Fried tofu and green onion bound with egg — a Kyoto original
items.note: Named after Mt. Kinugasa in northwest Kyoto. Abura-age and lots of green onion, set into the broth with egg. Purely local — you won't find it outside the city. There's a rice-bowl version, 衣笠丼, further down.

items.en: Egg dropped into a thick gingered broth
items.note: けいらん (written 鶏卵, 'hen's egg') is the Kyoto noodle-shop name for egg stirred into an ankake broth with plenty of grated ginger — soothing, thick and very warming. Another dish that barely exists outside Kyoto.

items.en: Noodles with an assortment of simmered toppings
items.note: An old Kyoto/Osaka noodle-shop dish borrowed from Nagasaki's shippoku banquet cuisine: a spread of toppings arranged over the noodles — typically kamaboko fishcake, shiitake, greens and fu (wheat gluten). The archaic spelling 志っぽく on the card is a nice sign of the shop's age.

items.en: Noodles in a thick starchy broth with mushroom and fishcake
items.note: のっぺい (written 濃餅/能平) is a starch-thickened soup found all over Japan; here it's a fuller ankake with shiitake, kamaboko and ginger.

なんば (namba) is Kansai shorthand for 長ねぎ, the fat white long onion — from Naniwa/Namba in Osaka, historically famous for growing it. So 'tori namba' = chicken and negi. Tokyo calls the same dish 鴨南蛮/鶏南蛮.

items.en: Chicken and egg with long onion
items.note: 親子 = 'parent and child', i.e. chicken plus egg — the same joke as oyakodon.
他人 = 'strangers' — beef and egg are not related, so it's the deliberate opposite of oyako. A very Kansai piece of wordplay.
In Kansai 肉 ('meat') without qualification means beef. Thin slices simmered in sweet soy.

items.en: Noodles with prawn tempura on top
items.note: Tempura batter is wheat flour and it's fried in a shared fryer. 天とじうどん (¥800) is the same tempura bound into the broth with egg.

items.en: Soba with a whole sweet-simmered herring — Kyoto's signature bowl
items.note: The dish Kyoto is known for. A dried Pacific herring (身欠きにしん) rehydrated and simmered for hours in sweet soy until the bones dissolve, laid on soba. Invented in Kyoto in 1882 because the landlocked city relied on dried fish from Hokkaido. If you eat one thing here that says 'Kyoto', this is it.
Originally a Nagasaki dish; in a Kyoto neighbourhood noodle shop it lands as noodles under a load of stir-fried vegetables and meat or seafood. Ask what's in it if it matters.

items.en: Udon simmered and served in its own clay pot
items.note: 鍋焼きうどん — cooked and brought to the table in a small earthenware pot, still boiling, usually with prawn tempura, an egg, chicken, kamaboko and mushrooms. The most substantial thing on the menu and a winter order. The pot is dangerously hot.

Curry udon/soba: Japanese curry loosened with dashi and thickened with starch, poured over the noodles. Splashes — everyone gets it on their shirt. きつねカレー (fried tofu) ¥700, 鳥カレー (chicken) ¥780. Japanese curry roux is flour-based.

items.en: Summer-only chilled Chinese noodles with a tart dressing
items.note: 季節の部 = the seasonal section. Cold noodles under strips of ham, egg, cucumber and so on with a soy-vinegar dressing — a Japanese summer institution. Also here: ざるそば (chilled soba on a bamboo mat with a dipping cup) ¥700, 冷やしうどん ¥700, 冷やしきつね ¥780.

items.en: Rice bowl: fried tofu and green onion set with egg
items.note: 丼 (don/donburi) = a bowl of rice with something cooked over it. This is Kyoto's own donburi and the one to try — the same abura-age and negi as the udon, simmered in dashi and bound with egg over rice. Cheap, local, and almost unknown outside the city.

items.en: Rice bowl: fishcake and onion set with egg
items.note: 木の葉 = 'tree leaves' — the thin slices of kamaboko fishcake floating in the egg are supposed to look like fallen leaves. Another Kansai-only bowl. The rest of the rice list: きつね丼 (fried tofu) ¥680, 玉子丼 (plain egg) ¥680, 天婦羅丼 (tempura) ¥750, 親子丼 (chicken and egg) ¥800, 他人丼 (beef and egg) ¥800, 天とじ丼 (tempura with egg) ¥800, 牛丼 (beef) ¥800.

items.ja: ライス　小 / 中 / 大
items.en: Plain white rice — small / medium / large
items.note: Unseasoned steamed rice, genuinely gluten-free and vegan as served. The card notes that all the rice used is grown in Shiga prefecture. Beer (ビール) is ¥550.

kyr_chuka_ryori_ban.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Core prices (ramen ¥300, chahan ¥360, set ¥600, chuka-don ¥400, tenshin-han ¥400) were confirmed by first-hand visits in 2026; a customer who asked in Feb 2026 was told by the owners that they have never raised prices. The longer item list comes from the shop's own handwritten outdoor board, photographed some years ago — treat those figures as indicative.

items.note: Thin straight noodles in a light clear soy broth, topped with thin-sliced pork chashu, bean sprouts and chopped green onion. ¥300 is not a typo — this shop deliberately prices for Kyoto University students and has held these prices for decades. Ordered together with fried rice it becomes the ¥600 set below, which is what most people get.

Kansai says yakimeshi where Tokyo says chahan (炒飯) — same dish, wok-fried rice with egg, pork and spring onion. Portions here are roughly twice what a normal shop serves; recent visitors report ¥350–360. Seasoned with wheat-based soy sauce.

items.ja: ラーメンやきめしセット
items.note: The order to point at if you can't read anything else. A full bowl of ramen plus a full plate of fried rice — both 'regular' size, both described by 2026 visitors as more than double a normal Kyoto shop's portion. One order per person; sharing a single order between two people is not allowed.

items.en: Chuka-don — stir-fried vegetables and pork in thick sauce over rice
items.note: A rice bowl under a glossy corn-starch-thickened stir-fry: bean sprouts, cabbage, Chinese leaf, carrot and a little pork. Confirmed at ¥400 by a February 2026 visitor. The sauce is built on wheat-brewed soy sauce.

items.en: Tenshin-han — crab-style omelette over rice with thick sauce
items.note: The shop's legendary dish. A flat omelette (here with cabbage folded in) laid over rice and flooded with a soy-and-vinegar ankake gravy. The standard size arrives in a ramen bowl holding an estimated 500 g of rice — a diner in 2010 recorded the 'large' at a 30 cm bowl. The menu states 大盛 (omori, large) is refused to first-timers, and a smaller 小 (ko) size is a little cheaper. Do not order it alongside another dish on a first visit; the staff will warn you.

items.en: Gomoku soba — ramen under a mixed meat-and-vegetable topping
items.note: 五目 literally means 'five things' and just signals a mixed topping — pork, squid or shrimp, cabbage, carrot, kikurage — spooned over the noodles in a thickened sauce. Price from the shop's outdoor board; verify.

items.en: Champon — Nagasaki-style noodles in a cloudy vegetable-and-seafood soup
items.note: Nagasaki's contribution to Japanese-Chinese cooking: everything (pork, seafood, cabbage, bean sprouts) is stir-fried in the wok, then soup is poured straight in and the noodles cooked in it, so the broth is milky and vegetable-sweet. Price from the outdoor board; verify.

Wheat noodles fried on the flat-top with pork and vegetables. At a machi-chuka like this it is usually the savoury soy-seasoned Chinese version rather than the sweet brown-sauce festival kind. Price from the outdoor board; verify.

items.en: Agesoba — crisp deep-fried noodles under thick sauce (kata-yakisoba)
items.note: The noodles are deep-fried into a crisp nest, then a thick pork-and-vegetable ankake is ladled over so it softens as you eat. Elsewhere in Japan this is called かた焼きそば (kata-yakisoba). One Kyoto University regular says agesoba is the only thing they ever order here. Price from the outdoor board; verify.

The standard fried rice with Japanese curry powder folded through. Japanese curry powder blends are usually wheat-free but the roux and soy sauce in the wok are not — ask. Price from the outdoor board; verify.
Fried rice reddened with tomato ketchup — a Showa-era Japanese comfort dish, essentially the filling of an omurice without the omelette. Price from the outdoor board; verify.

Pork is dusted in flour or starch, deep-fried, then tossed with onion, pepper and pineapple or carrot in a sweet vinegar sauce. The coating and the sauce both normally contain wheat. Price from the outdoor board; verify.

Marinated in soy, garlic and ginger, dredged in flour or potato starch and deep-fried. Also shows up as the 日替一品 (higawari ippin, daily side) inside the set meals. Price from the outdoor board; verify.
Cabbage, bean sprouts, carrot and onion hit hard in the wok. Usually has pork or pork fat in it and is finished with soy sauce, so ask on both counts. Price from the outdoor board; verify.
Ordered and eaten by a 2026 visitor alongside ramen and tenshin-han, but not printed on the outdoor board photo, so the price is unknown. Wheat wrapper, soy-based dipping sauce.

items.en: Set meal — main dish with rice, soup and a daily side
items.note: The illuminated sign outside reads 定食 520円より (teishoku, from ¥520); a 2024 visitor recorded ¥580–600. The wall inside is papered with the current combinations. A typical one pairs fried rice, a bowl of ramen and a rotating daily side such as kara-age.

items.en: Genghis Khan bowl — griddled mutton and vegetables over rice
items.note: ジンギスカン (jingisukan) is Hokkaido's soy-and-fruit-marinated grilled mutton with onion and cabbage; here it is served over rice. The price on the board photo is cut off at the edge of the frame.

items.en: 'Stamina' bowl — garlicky pork and vegetables over rice
items.note: スタミナ on a Japanese menu always means garlic, usually plus pork and nira (garlic chives) in a punchy soy sauce. Price cut off in the board photo.
Japanese curry over rice. Japanese curry roux is thickened with wheat flour almost without exception. Price cut off in the board photo.
Confirmed at ¥380 by a February 2026 visitor who ordered a 生中 (nama-chu, medium draught) with a chuka-don. Barley beer is not gluten-free.
Price read off the shop's own outdoor board; verify.

kyr_ramen_kura.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. The ¥690/¥790/¥890 ramen tier was transcribed from the in-store menu at opening (March 2024) and independently re-confirmed by diners in September 2025 and June 2026.

items.ja: 京出汁醤油らーめん つぼみ
items.note: The three ramen are named after a flower opening: つぼみ (tsubomi, bud) = no pork, 五分咲き (gobuzaki, half-bloom) = half a bowl of pork, 満開 (mankai, full bloom) = pork covering the whole surface. The broth is unusual for a ramen shop — kombu and dried fish with shiro-dashi, honjozo soy and mirin, closer to a Kyoto udon broth than a ramen one, with a slick of black mayu (burnt-garlic oil) on top. Toppings are Kujo negi and 油かす (abura-kasu, crisp-fried beef intestine, a Kansai speciality). Noodles are flat, wide, hand-crumpled and made by Kyoto's Menya Teigaku.

items.ja: 京出汁醤油らーめん 五分咲き
items.en: Kyoto-dashi soy ramen, 'half bloom' (half a bowl of chashu)
items.note: The middle size: paper-thin pork belly chashu laid over half the bowl. A diner in September 2025 paid ¥790, so the opening price still stands.

items.ja: 京出汁醤油らーめん 満開
items.en: Kyoto-dashi soy ramen, 'full bloom' (chashu covering the bowl)
items.note: The signature. Thin-cut pork belly is laid out in a full 360° circle like flower petals, hiding the noodles — a very Kyoto way of serving chashu. Confirmed at ¥890 in June 2026.

items.ja: 京出汁細うどん 京都九条ねぎ
items.en: Thin udon in Kyoto dashi with Kujo spring onion
items.note: The premises also runs a morning udon service, and those bowls stayed on the all-day menu. 九条ねぎ (Kujo negi) is Kyoto's own sweet, soft, hollow green onion — sweeter and less harsh than ordinary negi and the local point of pride. Broth is the same kombu-and-dried-fish Kyoto dashi, so not vegan.

items.ja: 京出汁細うどん 大阪炙り油かす
items.en: Thin udon in Kyoto dashi with seared abura-kasu
items.note: 油かす (abura-kasu) is beef intestine slowly fried until the fat renders out and it turns into crisp, chewy, intensely savoury nuggets — a southern-Osaka speciality that dissolves richness into the broth. If you like tripe or chicharrón you will like this.

items.ja: ねぎ＆油かす（ハーフ＆ハーフ）
items.en: Half-and-half udon: Kujo onion on one side, abura-kasu on the other
items.note: Can't choose — this splits the bowl. (The same write-up quotes ¥690 in its running text and ¥740 in the transcribed menu table; expect ¥740.)

items.ja: 冷やしつけ麺 あご疲れらぁ油そば
items.en: Chilled dipping noodles with a fiery chilli-oil dip and a raw egg yolk
items.note: つけ麺 (tsukemen) means the noodles come cold and naked and you dip them, a few strands at a time, into a small bowl of concentrated sauce. This one is modelled on Tokyo's cult shop Minatoya: udon-thick chilled noodles, a raw egg on top and a dip that is already hot before you touch it. The staff's recommended way is to stir in two more spoons of the house chilli oil until it is as hot as you can stand, then let the egg soften it. Kujo negi and abura-kasu go in too. Name is a joke — 'jaw fatigue', because the noodles are that chewy. Seasonal availability varies; ¥990 recorded June 2025.
A 2026 diner paid ¥940 total for 五分咲き with Kujo negi added, implying roughly ¥150 for the topping — but that is arithmetic, not a printed price, so check the table card.
Added by a 2026 diner to the tsukemen; price not published anywhere reachable.

items.en: How to order here — read this before anything else
items.section: システム / How it works
items.note: There is no shopfront. Take a wooden seat-number tag from beside the door to the right of the bolognese restaurant BIGOLI, walk into BIGOLI, say you're here for ramen, and you'll be led out the back to a converted kura (storehouse). Order on the black rotary telephone in the room — say your dish number and your seat number. Pay yourself into the open cash tray and take your own change; write your own receipt if you want one. Cash only. Clear your bowl and wipe the table on the way out and you take ¥10 back out of the change tray. Table condiments for mid-bowl adjustment: house chilli paste, house chilli oil, Chidori vinegar, shichimi and sansho.

kyr_ramenya_tamin.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. ¥900/¥1,000/¥1,100 for regular/large/extra-large was consistent across 2025 and early-2026 visits, but a July 2026 diner recorded ¥1,200 for a 200 g regular — portions and prices appear to have been re-cut, so treat these as a guide only.

items.note: 濃厚 (noko) means 'thick/concentrated' and here it is meant literally — a chicken-and-pork broth boiled down until it is closer to gravy than soup, sometimes signposted とりとん (toriton = tori chicken + ton pork). 並 (nami) is the regular size, historically 160 g of very thick wavy noodles, reported at 200 g in 2026. What arrives is mostly meat: two thick rare-ish pork shoulder slices plus one enormous folded belly chashu about 3 cm thick, charcoal-seared, plus menma, a mound of Kujo negi and green onion. Several diners describe it as heavier going than a proper Jiro bowl.

大盛 (omori) is the standard Japanese word for a large portion — you will meet it on every menu in the country. Here it buys 250 g of noodles. Given how rich the broth is, regulars advise stopping at this size.

items.en: Thick-broth ramen, extra large (350 g noodles)
items.note: 特盛 (tokumori) is a step above omori. A seasoned big-eater who regularly clears 400 g elsewhere described finishing this as 'a miracle'. Leaving food unfinished is frowned on here — order down, not up.

Cold thick straight noodles served dry, dipped into a hot concentrated pork-and-seafood sauce. Two slabs of rare pork shoulder and two cubes of braised belly come in the dip, seared just before serving. A April 2026 diner said 250 g ate like 400 g.

items.en: Chuka soba — the light, old-fashioned soy ramen
items.note: The shop's second pillar and the exact opposite of the noko bowl: a clear soy broth in the plain Showa-era idiom. The owner writes on his own blog that Kujo negi is essential to this one and pairs with it perfectly. No published price found.

items.ja: まぜそば タルタル（並 250g）
items.en: Brothless mixed noodles with house tartare sauce
items.note: まぜそば (mazesoba) has no soup — thick noodles sit in a pool of concentrated tare at the bottom of the bowl and you stir hard from underneath before eating. This version is topped with fried garlic chips, garlicky pork, house tartare sauce and shiraga-negi (fine white onion threads); the sweet tare against the sour tartare is the point.

items.en: Chilled ramen (summer only, ~10 bowls a day)
items.note: The owner's summer bowl and deliberately the reverse of everything else he cooks: a clear, de-fatted chicken-kombu-niboshi-katsuo broth with a complex salt tare (three salts, seven dashi, three soy sauces, a touch of sesame oil), medium-thick straight noodles, plus rolled roast pork, cold-cooked chicken breast and an ajitama. He posts on his own blog that it is capped at about ten servings a day and runs to the end of August — go early.

items.en: Cold noodles with vinegared sauce (summer only)
items.note: Japan's national summer noodle dish: chilled noodles under strips of toppings with a sharp sweet-sour soy-and-vinegar dressing. The owner rotates the toppings by what he can buy — rolled pork chashu is fixed, then variously pea shoots, paprika, Kujo negi, low-temperature chicken chashu and cherry tomatoes.

items.en: Chilled brothless mixed noodles (limited run, launched Aug 2026)
items.note: Announced on the shop's own blog on 18 August 2026, on a bespoke noodle he can only make in small numbers. He asks people who want it to come soon after opening.

items.en: Griddled ramen — steam-fried noodles in a soy-based sauce
items.note: An occasional limited item the owner documents himself: 300 g of noodles steam-griddled in a house soy sauce, topped with melting belly pork, negi and menma. He says it is seasoned to eat as-is, but regulars add a little of the counter garlic and curry powder for a mid-bowl change.

items.en: 'Dutch' dipping noodles, made with thin round noodles (summer limited)
items.note: Launched 10 August 2026. Unusually for tsukemen, it uses a thin round noodle rather than a thick one, because the owner wanted something that slips down in the heat.

味玉／味たま (ajitama) appears on virtually every ramen menu in Japan: a soft-centred egg steeped in soy tare. Here it is deliberately left plain-tasting so it works as a break from the very heavy broth. Marinade is soy-based.

Priced at ¥100 in a 2021 visit — many small pieces, lightly seasoned, meant to be dropped onto rice or dunked in the broth. Side dishes are sometimes restricted when the shop is busy; a sign asks you not to over-order.

items.en: Half portion of plain white rice
items.note: ¥50 in 2021. Plain unseasoned gohan is one of the very few genuinely gluten-free, vegan things in a ramen shop — but the counter staff will check you can actually finish it before they'll sell it to you. Watch that the scoop hasn't been in anything else.

items.ja: お持ち帰り（テイクアウト）
items.en: Takeaway kit of the thick-broth ramen
items.note: Roughly weekly the shop runs a takeaway-only day. The pack holds broth, noodles (deliberately over-portioned so you can do a second helping), meat and negi; two portions of the braised belly are included so one can go on rice as a donburi. Announced on the shop's X account.

items.en: How this shop works — read before you queue
items.section: システム / How it works
items.note: Five counter seats, one man cooking and washing alone, cash only, pay first (ticket system). Opening days are irregular and are announced only on the shop's X account (@msKWm5lPlwGCcxA) and his blog — people report being turned away five visits running. House rules are posted at the door and are enforced: wait to be called rather than walking straight in when a seat frees up, don't over-order sides, don't leave food. Limited items often sell out within an hour of opening.

kyr_kanton_ryori_heian.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Every figure below is read directly off the shop's own printed menu card, photographed in July 2022. A 2025 write-up quotes karashi-soba at ¥1,000 against the card's ¥900, so assume roughly 10% higher across the board today.

items.en: Karashi soba — ramen under a thick sauce sharpened with vinegar and Japanese mustard
items.note: The dish people cross Kyoto for, and a Kyoto-only genre descended from the legendary Hoomi lineage. It looks like an ordinary ankake chuka-soba, but rice vinegar and 和辛子 (wa-garashi, Japanese yellow mustard — hot in the nose like wasabi, not on the tongue like chilli) are whisked into the sauce, so the first mouthful goes straight up your sinuses before the gentle chicken broth catches up. Chicken, prawn, bamboo shoot and lettuce in the sauce. You choose the mustard level, and the levels are named after school grades: 中学 (chugaku, middle school = mild), 高校 (koko, high school = standard), 大学 (daigaku, university = strong). Beginners have successfully asked for 小学 (shogaku, primary school) and been looked after.

items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: Along with the karashi soba, the dish the regulars insist on. Wheat pastry, deep-fried.

items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: Flour-dusted deep-fried pork tossed in a sweet vinegar sauce with vegetables. Also available as one of the ¥1,000 lunch sets.

items.en: Happosai — 'eight-treasure' stir-fry in a light thick sauce
items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: The Cantonese all-rounder: pork, squid, prawn, quail egg, Chinese leaf, bamboo shoot, kikurage and carrot stir-fried and bound in a pale starch-thickened sauce. Order it with rice and you have effectively made yourself a chuka-don.

items.en: Chinjao rosu — shredded beef and green pepper stir-fry
items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: 青椒肉絲 — matchsticks of beef and green pepper (and usually bamboo shoot) fried fast in oyster and soy sauce. The most expensive stir-fry on the card, which tells you the beef is not an afterthought.
The house's undecorated bowl, and the base the karashi soba is built on: a clean chicken-bone soy broth with firm Chinese-style wheat noodles. Also offered as a ¥1,000 lunch set.
Kansai's word for chahan. It's what comes on the plate in the ¥1,000 lunch sets too. Wheat-brewed soy sauce and egg.
The soft-fried version: noodles loosened in the wok with pork and vegetables and seasoned with soy, not the sweet sauce of festival stalls.

items.en: Agesoba — crisp deep-fried noodles under thick sauce
items.note: Known elsewhere as かた焼きそば (kata-yakisoba). The noodles go into the fryer until they set into a crisp raft, then the same eight-treasure ankake is poured over — half the pleasure is the two textures as the sauce soaks in.

items.en: Gomoku soba — ramen with a mixed meat-and-vegetable topping
items.note: 五目 = 'five items', shorthand for a generous mixed topping. Soup version, so the sauce sits on top of a broth rather than replacing it.

items.en: Kanton-men — soup ramen under a Cantonese-style thick sauce
items.note: The house style in one bowl, and where the shop's name comes from (廣東 = Canton). Noodles in clear soup, then an ankake of vegetables and seafood ladled over the top so the bowl stays scalding to the last mouthful.
Everywhere else in Japan this is written チャーシュー麺 (chashu-men) — the plain ramen with the pork piled on. Same idea, older wording.
The banquet dish, in a bowl. Note this is real shark fin — decline if that matters to you.
海鮮 (kaisen) = seafood; prawn, squid, scallop and the like over noodles.
〈夏期のみ〉 printed beside it means summer only. In a Japanese-Chinese shop this is the vinegared cold-noodle plate (hiyashi-chuka style), not Korean naengmyeon.
〈冬期のみ〉 = winter only. Silky pork-filled wheat wrappers floating in clear broth.

items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: Winter only. Tofu and minced pork in a chilli-bean sauce. Contains pork and fermented wheat-based bean pastes even when it looks vegetarian.

items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: エビチリ is a Japanese-Chinese standard: prawns in a ketchup-and-chilli-bean sauce, milder and sweeter than the Sichuan original.

items.section: 一品料理 / À la carte
items.note: The closest thing to a vegetable plate on the card, but assume pork or pork fat and soy sauce unless told otherwise.

Preserved duck egg — jet-black translucent white, dark green creamy yolk, ammoniac and rich. Served cold in wedges, often with a little vinegar or ginger; a drinking snack, not a starter to fill up on.
Shredded salted jellyfish, rinsed and dressed with vinegar and sesame oil — crunchy and cool, barely any flavour of its own. The priciest starter on the card, so it is presumably a generous plate.
Steamed rather than fried, wrapped in a thin wheat skin left open at the top.
Cold poached or steamed chicken, sliced, usually under a sesame or spring-onion-and-ginger sauce. Sauce is soy-based.
Beaten egg threaded through hot chicken broth.
Unseasoned steamed white rice — the one genuinely gluten-free, genuinely vegan thing on this menu, as long as nothing is poured over it and the scoop is clean.

items.ja: シャーベット〈ゆず・ライチ〉
items.note: Yuzu is Japan's fragrant sour citrus; the lychee is the Cantonese classic. Confirm no dairy or honey if that matters.

items.en: Lunch set — a main plus fried rice, soup and small sides
items.note: The A-board out front reads お昼の定食 12時〜2時 いずれも1,000円 — lunch sets, 12:00 to 14:00, all ¥1,000. The photographs on the board show the main dish plus a plate of fried rice, a soup, a small side and pickles or fruit, and the choices are built from the à-la-carte list (sweet-and-sour pork, ramen, fried chicken, yakisoba, stir-fried vegetables, happosai and similar). The small print on the board was not fully legible in the photograph, so confirm the exact list on the day.

items.ja: 平安特製お弁当〈ごはん〉／〈焼き飯〉
items.en: Heian's own bento box — with plain rice or with fried rice
items.section: お持ち帰りのみ / Takeaway only
items.note: Marked ◆お持ち帰りのみ◆ (takeaway only) at the foot of the menu card — you cannot eat it in. ¥1,100 with plain rice, ¥1,200 with fried rice.

kyr_mazemen_puruda.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. All figures are from July 2025, within a month of the shop's grand opening; no full menu board has been published anywhere reachable, so this is a partial list.

items.en: Mazemen, regular — brothless noodles you stir yourself
items.note: まぜ麺／まぜそば has no soup: a concentrated secret soy tare with lard and chicken oil sits under the noodles and you stir hard from the bottom of the bowl before you start. The noodles are Menya Teigaku's thick, flat, wavy wholemeal-flecked type with real chew. Toppings as served: a big slab of rare pork shoulder chashu, thick-cut menma, Korean gim seaweed and shiraga-negi (fine white onion threads). 並 (nami) is the regular size. Chilli oil sits on the counter for a mid-bowl change of direction.

items.ja: まぜ麺 全部のせ 並
items.note: 全部のせ (zenbu-nose, 'all loaded on') is the standard Japanese ramen-menu phrase for the version with every topping — here that includes kimchi and Korean seaweed alongside the pork and egg. If you only order one thing and want to see what the shop can do, this is it.

温泉玉子 (onsen tamago) is cooked slowly at low temperature so the white stays loose and the yolk sets to a jelly — the opposite of a poached egg. Break it into the noodles and it turns the tare creamy. Worth the ¥100 on a brothless bowl.
Korean-style gim — sesame-oiled and salted rather than plain Japanese nori, which fits the shop's Korean side. Plain seaweed itself is fine on both counts, but check for shared oil if you're strict.

items.en: Finishing rice — a scoop of rice to mop the bowl
items.note: The ritual end of any mazemen: when the noodles are gone, ask for rice (elsewhere written 追い飯 oimeshi) and stir it through the tare and fat left at the bottom. A July 2025 diner did exactly this here. The rice itself is plain, but once it hits the leftover tare it is neither gluten-free nor vegan. Price not published.

items.section: システム / How it works
items.note: MAZEMEN プルダ only exists at lunchtime — 11:00 to 14:00, closed Mondays. The same room turns into the Korean restaurant 韓杯房 プルダ at night, and the mazemen is NOT served in the evening. Don't confuse the two names when searching: the Korean brand has its own listings and its own, different menu. Three minutes from Kyoto Station's Hachijo (south) exit.

kyr_toyojiro.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Prices are from first-hand visits between December 2024 and June 2025; the ordering screen itself is behind a QR code and could not be read directly.

items.ja: 煮込み肉入りアブララーメン（ぼっかけ二郎麺）
items.en: Jiro-style ramen with braised beef sinew and wagyu fat
items.note: The whole point of this shop. Standard Jiro-style ramen is built on pork back-fat; here the fat is A5 wagyu from Okazaki Farm and the meat is 48-month-old female beef, which is why the price is triple a normal Jiro bowl. ぼっかけ (bokkake) is a Kobe speciality — beef sinew and offal simmered soft in sweet white miso. The result is much lighter and cleaner than a pork Jiro bowl but still very rich. Staff will tell you to stir it up from the bottom and eat fast, because beef fat firms up as it cools. Thick noodles by Menya Teigaku. Several diners describe it as essentially a soupless bowl.

items.ja: 肉抜きアブララーメン
items.en: The same bowl without the braised beef
items.note: 肉抜き (niku-nuki) means 'meat removed'. Same noodles, same wagyu-fat seasoning, ¥300 less. There are only these two base bowls; everything else is a topping.

items.en: Choose your base: soy sauce or salt
items.note: You'll be asked this when you order. 醤油 (shoyu) is the soy-sauce base — deeper, darker, the default for most people. 塩 (shio) is the salt base — cleaner, and it lets the beef flavour through more. No price difference.

Also asked at ordering, no surcharge either way. This is much gentler than a real Jiro shop, where the small is already an ordeal. Given how rich the beef fat is, 200 g is plenty even for a big eater.

items.ja: ニンニク あり／なし
items.note: At a proper Ramen Jiro the counter staff bark a call as your bowl is built and you answer with a string of words — ニンニク (ninniku, raw chopped garlic), ヤサイ (yasai, extra bean sprouts and cabbage), アブラ (abura, extra back-fat), カラメ (karame, stronger seasoning), each optionally with マシ (mashi, more) or マシマシ (mashi-mashi, lots more). Here the shop is far gentler and only asks the garlic question. Answer あり (ari, yes) or なし (nashi, no) — or just nod or shake your head. Diners note the garlic is worth having if you're not going back to work.
全部乗せ is the standard phrase for 'give me every topping'. ¥450 on top of the bowl price, recorded December 2024.

items.en: Finishing rice — a scoop of rice for the bottom of the bowl
items.note: 追い飯 (oimeshi) is the closing move on any thick or brothless bowl: when the noodles are gone you ask for rice and stir it into the fat, tare and scraps of beef left behind. Recorded at ¥150 in June 2025. The rice is plain but everything you mix it into is not.

items.ja: ランチ ミネラルウォーター飲み放題
items.note: Important and unusual: water is NOT free here. Multiple diners were caught out — you either buy the ¥150 lunchtime all-you-can-drink water or buy a bottled drink. Budget for it, and expect to want it with a bowl this rich.

items.ja: 限定X（神戸牛の牛骨ラーメン 塩）
items.romaji: gentei X — Kobe-gyu no gyukotsu raamen, shio
items.en: Members-only limited bowl: Kobe beef bone ramen, salt base
items.note: A separate limited bowl you have to sign up in advance to order — a clear salt ramen built on Kobe beef bones rather than pork or chicken, described as tasting more like drinking a fine consommé than a ramen. Price not published.

items.en: How this shop works — read before you sit down
items.section: システム / How it works
items.note: TOYOJIRO is not its own restaurant — it borrows the counter of the tuna-and-wagyu izakaya とよ田 (Toyota) at Yaoyacho 112-2, and staff will ask whether you're here for ramen or for the izakaya. Say ramen: choosing the izakaya route obliges you to take the お通し (otoshi, compulsory seat-charge appetiser) and one drink. Ordering is by QR code at the counter, paid on the spot; PayPay and cards work and cash is accepted for the ramen side. Roughly 5 minutes on foot from Hankyu Kyoto-Kawaramachi. Note this shop is Jiro-INSPIRED and has nothing to do with the Ramen Jiro chain — the chain's Kyoto branch is a different shop in Ichijoji with completely different prices.

kyr_menya_ichiki.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off a full-resolution photograph of the shop's own ticket machine dated 2026-04-22, the day it reopened at the new Murasakino address, so this is the newest possible card.

items.note: The house bowl and the whole reason the shop exists. Kyoto 白味噌 (shiro-miso) is pale, soft and noticeably sweet — nothing like the dark, salty red miso of Sapporo. Thick noodles, smoked chashu, a heap of green onion. Order this first if you only eat one.

items.ja: 京の白味噌 ゴマ豆乳らーめん
items.en: White-miso ramen with sesame and soy milk
items.note: Same sweet white-miso base loosened with soy milk and ground sesame — rounder and nuttier, almost like a tan-tan without the heat. Soy milk does not make it vegan; the broth is not.

items.ja: 京の白味噌 貝だしらーめん
items.note: The pricier signature: white miso cut with 貝だし, a clam/shellfish stock that adds a clean briny edge to the sweetness. The shop flags this one as its recommendation.

items.ja: 京の白味噌チャーシュー麺
items.en: White-miso ramen loaded with extra pork
items.note: チャーシュー麺 (chashu-men) anywhere in Japan means the standard bowl buried under extra slices of braised pork. Here the pork is smoked.

items.ja: 京の白味噌 ゴマ豆乳チャーシュー麺
items.en: Sesame soy-milk white-miso ramen with extra pork
items.note: The sesame–soy-milk bowl with the extra-pork treatment.

替え玉 (kaedama) is a second nest of noodles dropped into the soup you have left. Buy the ticket up front at the machine, then hand it over when your bowl is about a third full so the broth is still hot.
A whole extra nest. Same timing rule — order before the broth cools.

Also called 味玉 (ajitama). Boiled to a jammy centre then steeped in a soy-mirin marinade — the single most ordered topping in Japan. The marinade is soy-based, so it is not gluten-free unless the shop confirms otherwise.
A mound of sliced green onion. In Kyoto this is usually 九条ねぎ (Kujo negi), the local variety — thicker, sweeter and more tender than ordinary scallion, and a Kyoto vegetable in its own right.

湯葉 is the delicate skin lifted off the surface of simmering soy milk — a Kyoto temple-food speciality, and the most local thing you can add to a bowl here. It softens into the miso as you eat. Plain yuba is just soy, but ask whether it has been simmered in dashi or soy seasoning.
Genuinely plain steamed rice, unseasoned. The one safe order in a wheat-heavy shop — ask for it as-is, with no sauce and no soy poured over.

items.en: Rice bowl topped with smoked pork
items.note: Rice under slices of the same smoked chashu, with sauce. The standard ramen-shop side.
Boneless chicken marinated in soy and ginger, dusted in potato or wheat starch and deep-fried. Wheat in the marinade and a shared fryer.

items.ja: チャーシュー盛り合わせ
items.note: The chashu served on its own as a plate, to eat with a beer rather than on noodles.
The bundled add-on most people press after their ramen button — rice plus kara-age for less than buying both.

items.ja: チャーシュー丼＋唐揚げ
items.en: Pork rice bowl plus fried chicken
items.note: The hungry combination.
Beer-and-snack set, cheaper than the two apart.

items.ja: 瓶ビール＋チャーシュー盛り合わせ
items.note: The other beer set.
瓶 means bottle. Barley beer, so not gluten-free.
As expensive as the ramen — an unusual thing to find on a ramen ticket machine.

items.ja: ノンアルコールビール
items.note: Still brewed from barley malt despite having no alcohol.
Water is free and self-service from the counter, so you only need this if you want it.

kyr_menya_kagari_kiyamachi_t.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Taken from a photograph of the shop's current laminated tabletop MENU card dated 2026-06, the newest menu photo on its Tabelog page; the ¥950 tonkotsu price is independently confirmed by a dated June 2026 first-hand visit. An older 2018 board for this shop is still circulating online with ¥700 prices and a yuba ramen — it is obsolete, do not use it.

items.note: The card's own line: こってりなのに、くどくない — rich but not cloying. Creamy, salt-forward pork broth over thin straight noodles, heaped with Kujo green onion. The most-ordered bowl here.
鶏白湯 (tori-paitan) means chicken bones boiled hard until the broth turns opaque and thick. The card describes it as 鶏の旨味がつまったとろみスープ — a soup with body, packed with chicken savour.

items.ja: 焦がしニンニク 黒ラーメン
items.note: Black because of マー油 — garlic fried until it blackens, then blended into oil. Smoky, bitter-sweet, faintly coffee-like, and genuinely potent on the breath. The card promises you will be hooked after one bowl.

items.ja: 炙りチャーシューメン
items.note: On a separate wall sign rather than the main card, so check it is still up. 炙り means the pork slices are seared with a flame just before serving, so the fat edges caramelise.
大盛 (omori) = more noodles in the same bowl, added at the counter. The opposite, if you want less, is 少なめ (sukuname).

items.en: Upgrade any bowl to extra pork
items.note: Not a separate dish here but a surcharge on whichever ramen you chose, which buries it in extra slices. The card shows this price hand-corrected upward, so treat it as the current figure rather than a printed one.

items.en: Half a portion of extra noodles
items.note: 替玉 (kaedama) is the Kyushu-tonkotsu habit of ordering a fresh nest of noodles to finish the broth you have left. Ask while the soup is still hot.

items.en: A full portion of extra noodles
items.note: The full nest.

items.ja: ギョーザ 一人前6個
items.note: 一人前 means one serving; here that is six. Wheat wrappers, soy in the filling and in the dipping sauce.
Chopped chashu with Japanese mayonnaise over rice — the classic 3am order after drinking on Kiyamachi.
The chashu on its own, to go with a beer.
The jammy-yolked marinated egg — cheap here at ¥100, half what most shops charge. Soy marinade, so wheat unless confirmed.
小 = small. Unseasoned steamed rice, and the only genuinely gluten-free, vegan thing on this menu.
中 = medium. Same plain rice, larger bowl.
Barley beer.
酎ハイ (chuhai) is shochu spirit topped with soda — here with lemon. Shochu can be distilled from barley, so ask if that matters.
Japan's default mixed drink — whisky, soda, lots of ice.
You pick the base: 麦 (mugi) is barley, 芋 (imo) is sweet potato and earthier. Say 芋 to avoid barley.
各 (kaku) on the card means 'each' — either one is ¥200.

kyr_no_ko_tonkotsu_ramen_iwa.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. Read off full-resolution photographs of the shop's own ticket machine dated 2026-01, its street A-board (2026-01) and its in-store ordering card (2026-01); the ¥950 base ramen and the ¥100 spinach, ¥100 nori and ¥200 rice add-ons are re-confirmed unchanged by a dated August 2026 first-hand visit, so the card is still current.

items.note: The machine labels this ど定番!! 初めての方はまずこちら — the absolute standard, start here. 家系 (iekei) is the Yokohama style: heavy pork-bone-and-soy broth, thick chewy noodles, one slice of pork, spinach and sheets of nori. Comes with 1 chashu, 3 nori and spinach.

上 (jo) means 'upper grade'. The board itemises it: 煮豚1枚 (one braised pork slice), 燻製焼豚1枚 (one smoked pork slice), のり5枚 (5 nori), 味玉1個 (one marinated egg), spinach — ¥50 cheaper than buying those separately.
特上 = 'extra top'. Marked 店長のおすすめ (the manager's pick) and 200円お得 (¥200 of savings): 2 braised pork, 2 smoked pork, 5 nori, 1 marinated egg, double spinach.

Noodles served cold and naked with a separate bowl of concentrated broth to dunk them in, mouthful by mouthful. This one is finished with yuzu to cut the richness. The sign says 熱盛不可 — they will NOT serve the noodles warmed, so expect them chilled.

The shop's crossover: iekei broth under a Jiro-style mound of 300g of beansprouts and cabbage. 並 (nami) = regular, 180g of noodles. You get asked about garlic at the counter — see the ニンニク note below.
大 (dai) = large, 270g of noodles under the same 300g vegetable mountain. This is a lot of food; 並 defeats most people.

items.ja: ニンニク（なし／少なめ／普通／マシ／マシマシ）
items.romaji: ninniku: nashi / sukuname / futsuu / mashi / mashi-mashi
items.en: The garlic call on the Jiro bowl — free choice
items.note: On the 家二郎 only, staff ask how much raw crushed garlic you want. Answer with one word: なし (nashi, none), 少なめ (sukuname, a little), 普通 (futsuu, normal), マシ (mashi, extra), マシマシ (mashi-mashi, double extra). It is free and it is fierce — 普通 is already a heaped spoonful of raw garlic.

items.ja: 麺の硬さ・味の濃さ・脂の量
items.romaji: men no katasa / aji no kosa / abura no ryoo
items.en: The three iekei choices you are asked at ordering
items.note: The house card spells it out: when you order they ask three things, all free. 麺の硬さ (noodle firmness): 硬め katame / 普通 futsuu / 軟らかめ yawarakame. 味の濃さ (seasoning strength): 濃いめ koime / 普通 / 薄め usume. 脂の量 (fat): 多め oome / 普通 / 少なめ sukuname. If in doubt just say 普通 three times. The regulars' answer is かため、濃いめ、多め.
The standard bowl with the pork count maxed out.

items.en: Ramen with green onion and pork
items.note: ネギチャ is shop shorthand for a dressed pile of sliced green onion tossed with chopped chashu — sharp and fresh against the heavy broth.
キャベチャ = cabbage plus chashu, the same idea with shredded cabbage instead of onion.
The base bowl with 味玉 (ajitama) already in it.
大盛 (omori) = large. Bought as a separate ticket at the machine.

items.en: One slice of smoked roast pork
items.note: 枚 (mai) is the counter for flat things — one slice. The smoked version is the shop's own; it is what they lead with.
Iekei ritual: dunk a nori sheet until it goes limp, wrap a few noodles in it, eat. Plain roasted nori is gluten-free and vegan, though seasoned nori sometimes is not — these are plain.
The jammy marinated egg. Soy-based marinade means wheat by default.
背脂 (seabura) is pork back-fat, crumbled over the top so it melts into the surface of the broth. 50g is a serious amount — this is the button that makes the bowl heavy.
Blanched spinach is standard in iekei and the cheapest way to make the bowl feel less punishing. Often blanched or dressed with dashi or soy, so ask.
The onion-and-chashu mix added to any bowl.
The cabbage-and-chashu version.
The cheapest button on the machine. Raw white onion, diced, for a bit of bite.

items.en: Half portion of plain white rice
items.note: 半 = half. Plain unseasoned rice, and the honest gluten-free option here. Iekei tradition is to soak a nori sheet in the broth and eat it draped over the rice. Note the lunchtime sign: 11:00–15:00 rice is ¥100 off, so this drops to ¥50.

items.en: Full portion of plain white rice
items.note: The full bowl of plain rice; ¥100 between 11:00 and 15:00 under the lunchtime discount.

items.en: Green onion and pork rice bowl
items.note: 丼 (don) means a rice bowl with something on top.

items.ja: 炙りマヨキャベチャ丼
items.en: Seared mayo, cabbage and pork rice bowl
items.note: Marked NEW on the machine. Mayonnaise blowtorched until it browns, over cabbage and chashu on rice.
The shop's smoked chashu over rice, sold as its own dish.

items.ja: 瓶ビール（プレモル小瓶）
items.en: Small bottle of Premium Malt's beer
items.note: 小瓶 = small bottle. Barley beer.

kyr_aburasoba_daikakumei_kin.price_note: Prices approximate — may change. This shop runs TWO ticket-machine panels and swaps between them, so treat the lineup as unstable. The 油そば panel below is read off photographs from roughly 2025-09, corroborated by a dated August 2025 visit and by a May 2026 diner who ordered 「普通の油そば」, so it is still live. The あえ麺 panel (釜玉 / 肉みそ / 肉玉) is read off a separate photograph from roughly late 2025, and a 2026-04 reviewer describes the shop as having had a リニューアルオープン. Expect one of the two panels on any given visit; check before queueing.

items.en: Brothless noodles in tare and oil
items.note: There is no soup. A pool of soy tare and chilli-scented oil sits hidden in the bottom of the bowl under the noodles, with chashu, shredded nori, menma and sesame on top. The shop's own instructions: first splash 酢 (su, vinegar) and ラー油 (rayu, chilli oil) once or twice around the rim from the table bottles, then mix hard — flipping the noodles over — until the tare is evenly through and no dry patches remain. Only then start eating. They also suggest 黒酢 (black vinegar) as it pairs with the garlic.
半熟 (hanjuku) means half-cooked — a soft-boiled egg with a runny centre. Break it into the mix and the yolk turns the tare creamy.
肉盛り = a mound of meat. Four chashu slices instead of the standard two, fanned right across the bowl.

全部のせ (zenbu-nose) literally 'everything placed on' — the shop's own poster explains this one is the standard bowl plus a soft-boiled egg AND four chashu slices. If you can't read the machine and want the full experience, this is the button.

学生 (gakusei) = student. An orange band across the machine marks the 学割料金 (student rate) row — Ritsumeikan University is a few minutes away. The whole row is ¥100 off: 半熟玉子 ¥800, 肉盛り ¥900, 全部のせ ¥1,000. You need to be a student; expect to be asked.

From the second, あえ麺 (aemen, sauce-tossed noodle) panel. 釜玉 borrows the udon idea: hot noodles tossed straight with raw egg so it thickens into a carbonara-like coating, here with pork and sesame. The button notes you can swap 味ネギ for 花かつお (bonito flakes).

Minced pork cooked down with miso and chilli over the noodles with an egg yolk and chives. The button says the 肉みそ（辛） can be served 別皿 — on a separate plate — if you want to control the heat, and that a 釜玉 topping also suits it.
The top of the aemen panel — sliced pork blanketing the noodles with a yolk in the middle.

items.ja: 全あえ麺に玉子が入っております
items.romaji: zen aemen ni tamago ga haitte orimasu
items.en: Every aemen contains egg — tell staff if you can't have it
items.note: A printed strip runs the width of the aemen panel: 全あえ麺に玉子が入っておりますので苦手な方はスタッフにお申し出ください — every aemen has egg in it, so tell staff if that is a problem. Worth knowing before you press a button if you avoid egg.
The aemen panel has its own student row: 釜玉 ¥700, 肉みそ ¥850, 肉玉 ¥900.

The portion buttons sit at the very top of the machine, so press your bowl first and then one of these. 大盛 is the ordinary 'large'. On the aemen panel this is handled differently — a sign says ordering 並 (regular) lets you change up to 大盛 or W盛 free by asking staff.
Twice the noodles. Since there is no broth to fill you up, regulars say the standard size runs small and double is very manageable.
Three times the noodles, same price per step. Genuinely large. Present on both panels.

items.en: Lunch set — fried chicken plus rice
items.note: The small label under the button reads からあげ3つ・TKGか白ごはん: three pieces of fried chicken plus either the raw-egg rice or plain rice.

items.en: Value set — rice plus fried chicken
items.note: The aemen panel's equivalent: a bowl of rice and a portion of kara-age.
Plain unseasoned steamed rice — the one genuinely gluten-free and vegan item here, and priced the same on both panels. Keep it separate from the noodle bowl if that matters to you.

items.en: A 50g scoop of rice for the leftover sauce
items.note: The machine explains it: チョイ飯（50g）とは？食べ終わった油そばのタレにご飯を入れて食べるタレご飯 — a small scoop of rice you tip into the tare left in the bottom of the bowl once the noodles are gone, then stir and eat. This is the ending the shop wants you to have, and it costs ¥50. The rice itself is plain, but the sauce it soaks up is wheat soy.
Soy-and-ginger marinated chicken, starch-coated and deep-fried. Priced ¥250 on the aemen panel and ¥300 on the abura-soba panel, so expect either.

items.ja: ヤンニョム風 唐揚げ
items.note: On the aemen panel only. The same kara-age tossed in a 양념 (yangnyeom) sweet-garlic-chilli glaze. Gochujang normally contains wheat.

items.en: Fries plus two pieces of fried chicken
items.note: On the abura-soba panel. The machine spells it out: ポテト＆唐揚げ2ヶ — potato fries and two kara-age, sharing the fryer.
炙り = flame-seared. Chashu blowtorched over rice.
On the aemen panel. Chopped chashu with Japanese mayonnaise over rice.

TKG is the standard abbreviation for 卵かけご飯 — a raw egg cracked over hot rice and stirred, usually with a splash of soy. A completely ordinary Japanese breakfast, and here the recommended finish: the shop's poster says pour the leftover tare in too and add the raw egg for the perfect ending. On both panels at ¥200.

items.ja: トッピング 半熟玉子／生卵
items.en: Add a soft-boiled egg, or a raw one
items.note: The pink-labelled row along the bottom of the machine is all toppings. 半熟玉子 (soft-boiled) is ¥100; 生卵 (nama-tamago, raw) is ¥50.
